questions.problem:
A function $f(x)$ has values according to the table below:

| $x$ | $-3$ | $-2$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $0.9$ | $0.4$ | $0.1$ | $0$ | $0.1$ | $0.4$ | $0.9$ |

Approximate ${f}^{′}(x)$ at the point $x=-1$ using a backward difference approximation.
questions.worked_solution:
We use the backward difference approximation formula

$$
{f}^{′}(x)≈\frac{f(x)-f(x-h)}{h}
$$

 

at the point $x=-1.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case, $h=1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(-1) & ≈\frac{f(-1)-f(-1-1)}{1} \\  & =\frac{f(-1)-f(-2)}{1} \\  & =\frac{0.1-0.4}{1} \\  & =-0.3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
An oil tank is leaking. The volume of oil in the tank, in liters, after $t$ hours is given by the function $q(t).$ The values of $q(t)$ for different values of $t$ are given in the table below:

| $t$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $q(t)$ | $200$ | $192$ | $186$ | $182$ | $180$ |

Approximate the rate at which the volume of oil in the tank is changing when $t=2$ using a backward difference approximation.
questions.worked_solution:
We use the backward difference approximation formula

$$
{q}^{′}(t)≈\frac{q(t)-q(t-h)}{h},
$$

 
at the time $t=2.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case $h=1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}^{′}(2) & ≈\frac{q(2)-q(2-1)}{1} \\  & =\frac{q(2)-q(1)}{1} \\  & =186-192 \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the rate of change of the volume is $-6$ liters per hour.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(16) & ≈\frac{f(16)-f(16-3)}{3} \\  & =\frac{f(16)-f(13)}{3} \\  & =\frac{21-15}{3} \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
A race car's position along a straight track, measured in meters from the starting line, is given by the function $s(t),$ where $t$ is the time in seconds. The values of $s(t)$ for different values of $t$ are given in the table below.

| $t$ | $1.2$ | $1.4$ | $1.6$ | $1.8$ | $2.0$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $s(t)$ | $1.3$ | $2.7$ | $2.9$ | $3.5$ | $5.0$ |

Approximate the velocity $s'(t)$ when $t=1.6$ using a backward difference approximation.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use the backward difference approximation formula

$$
s'(t) \approx \frac{s(t) - s(t-h)}{h}
$$

 

at the time $t=1.6.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case $h=0.2.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}^{′}(1.6) & ≈\frac{s(1.6)-s(1.6-0.2)}{0.2} \\  & =\frac{s(1.6)-s(1.4)}{0.2} \\  & =\frac{2.9-2.7}{0.2} \\  & =\frac{0.2}{0.2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So at the time $t=1.6,$ the velocity is approximately $1\, \textrm{m}/\textrm{s}.$

Approximate the marginal cost $C'(x)$ at the point $x=3$ using a backward difference approximation with step size $h=2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use the backward difference approximation formula

$$
C'(x) \approx \dfrac{C(x) - C(x-h)}{h},
$$

 
at the point $x=3.$ Applying the above formula with $x=3$ and $h=2$ gives

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
To approximate the derivative of a function, we can use the finite difference formula

$$
f'(x)\approx \frac{f(x) - f(x-h) }{h}
$$

for small values of the step size $h,$ with $h>0.$

This expression is known as the **backward difference approximation** because if $h>0$ then $x-h$ is a step behind $x$ (i.e., to the left). 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14194326/assets/ddc03ba86c8c343d5733b51444cec157182894b6d0c4fccb501b1dc3bca98f57.png)

As usual, the smaller the step size $h$ is, the better the approximation to $f'(x)$ we obtain.
tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
To approximate the derivative of a function, we can use the finite difference formula

$$
f'(x)\approx \frac{f(x) - f(x-h) }{h}
$$

for small values of the step size $h,$ with $h>0.$

This expression is known as the **backward difference approximation** because if $h>0$ then $x-h$ is a step behind $x$ (i.e., to the left). 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14194326/assets/ddc03ba86c8c343d5733b51444cec157182894b6d0c4fccb501b1dc3bca98f57.png)

As usual, the smaller the step size $h$ is, the better the approximation to $f'(x)$ we obtain.

tutorials.name: Derivation of the Formula
tutorials.problem:
Where does the formula for the backward difference come from? Remember that from the definition of derivative, we have the forward difference formula

$$
f'(x)\approx \frac{f(x+h) - f(x) }{h}
$$

for small values of  $h.$ 

Now, replacing $h$ with $-h$ in the formula above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ≈\frac{f(x-h)-f(x)}{-h} \\  & =\frac{f(x)-f(x-h)}{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

The step of replacing $h$ with $-h$ is equivalent to stepping a distance of $h$ to the left rather than to the right.
